### Architecture Decision
Treat the API layer as a contract boundary: typed requests/responses, cancellation, retries, auth, telemetry and normalized errors.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

```ts
} as const;
```

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **When might gRPC matter to a frontend architecture?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Treat the API layer as a contract boundary: typed requests/responses, cancellation, retries, auth, telemetry and normalized errors.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

```text
   ↓
```

### Architecture Decision
Treat the API layer as a contract boundary: typed requests/responses, cancellation, retries, auth, telemetry and normalized errors.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.

- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management

- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.

- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.

### Architecture Decision
Treat the API layer as a contract boundary: typed requests/responses, cancellation, retries, auth, telemetry and normalized errors.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

```ts
} as const;
```

## Question 99 — How should API contracts be tested?

**Module:** API Design  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐ Hard  
**Expected Time:** 45 mins  
**Experience:** 8–12 Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should API contracts be tested?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Treat the API layer as a contract boundary: typed requests/responses, cancellation, retries, auth, telemetry and normalized errors.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Configuration Example

```ts
  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```

I would choose state and rendering strategies based on the actual quality attributes, add caching and observability deliberately, secure trusted boundaries, and finish by explaining failure handling and trade-offs.

I would then walk through a representative request, explain failure recovery and describe how the design scales across traffic and teams. Finally, I would compare alternatives and identify the migration path.

### 5-Minute Deep Explanation
A strong Staff/Principal answer for **How would you design an enterprise API gateway/BFF boundary?** is not a technology checklist. It connects business goals to architecture. I would explicitly state assumptions, identify the highest-risk quality attributes, choose boundaries that minimize coupling, define server/client state ownership, design API and cache contracts, and explain security, accessibility and performance as first-class constraints. I would then model failure scenarios, observability and deployment. The final part is trade-offs: what we gain, what complexity we accept, what we defer, and how the architecture can evolve.

## Question 101 — How do you design a secure login flow?

**Module:** Authentication Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐ Hard  
**Expected Time:** 45 mins  
**Experience:** 8–12 Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How do you design a secure login flow?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Prefer secure, server-managed sessions or appropriately protected cookies over exposing long-lived secrets to JavaScript.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Configuration Example

```ts
  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```

## Question 104 — How should SSO work in an enterprise frontend?

**Module:** Authentication Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐ Hard  
**Expected Time:** 45 mins  
**Experience:** 8–12 Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should SSO work in an enterprise frontend?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Prefer secure, server-managed sessions or appropriately protected cookies over exposing long-lived secrets to JavaScript.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

```ts
  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```

### 30-Second Interview Answer
For **How should SSO work in an enterprise frontend?**, I would first clarify requirements and scale, then separate UI, domain, data and infrastructure boundaries. I would choose state and rendering strategies based on the actual quality attributes, add caching and observability deliberately, secure trusted boundaries, and finish by explaining failure handling and trade-offs.

### 2-Minute Interview Answer
The architecture for **How should SSO work in an enterprise frontend?** should begin with functional and non-functional requirements. I would define the React/Next.js application boundary, component and feature boundaries, state ownership, API/BFF contracts, caching, authentication, accessibility, performance and observability. I would then walk through a representative request, explain failure recovery and describe how the design scales across traffic and teams. Finally, I would compare alternatives and identify the migration path.

### 5-Minute Deep Explanation
A strong Staff/Principal answer for **How should SSO work in an enterprise frontend?** is not a technology checklist. It connects business goals to architecture. I would explicitly state assumptions, identify the highest-risk quality attributes, choose boundaries that minimize coupling, define server/client state ownership, design API and cache contracts, and explain security, accessibility and performance as first-class constraints. I would then model failure scenarios, observability and deployment. The final part is trade-offs: what we gain, what complexity we accept, what we defer, and how the architecture can evolve.

## Question 106 — What is silent refresh and when is it appropriate?

**Module:** Authentication Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐ Hard  
**Expected Time:** 45 mins  
**Experience:** 8–12 Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **What is silent refresh and when is it appropriate?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Prefer secure, server-managed sessions or appropriately protected cookies over exposing long-lived secrets to JavaScript.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

## Question 108 — How should protected routes be designed?

**Module:** Authentication Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐ Hard  
**Expected Time:** 45 mins  
**Experience:** 8–12 Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should protected routes be designed?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

```text
Observability

  └── Traces
```

### Architecture Decision
Prefer secure, server-managed sessions or appropriately protected cookies over exposing long-lived secrets to JavaScript.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

## Question 110 — How does ABAC differ from RBAC?

**Module:** Authentication Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐ Hard  
**Expected Time:** 45 mins  
**Experience:** 8–12 Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How does ABAC differ from RBAC?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Prefer secure, server-managed sessions or appropriately protected cookies over exposing long-lived secrets to JavaScript.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

```text
   ↓ failure
Health Check
   ↓
Traffic Shift
   ↓
Secondary Region
   ↓
Recovery Validation
```

### Architecture Decision
Prefer secure, server-managed sessions or appropriately protected cookies over exposing long-lived secrets to JavaScript.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

```ts
  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,

} as const;
```

### Functional Requirements

- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

- High availability and graceful degradation.

- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.

- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management

### Architecture Decision
Prefer secure, server-managed sessions or appropriately protected cookies over exposing long-lived secrets to JavaScript.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |

| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

```ts
} as const;
```

- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.

- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.

- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.

- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Architecture Decision
Prefer secure, server-managed sessions or appropriately protected cookies over exposing long-lived secrets to JavaScript.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Configuration Example

```ts
  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```
