### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should threat modeling be performed?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements

- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Architecture Decision
Security is defense in depth: browser controls, secure cookies, CSP, authorization, API security, dependency hygiene and observability.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Configuration Example
```ts
// Architecture-level configuration should be environment driven.
// Never place production secrets in client-side source.

  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```

## Question 296 — How should third-party scripts be governed?

**Module:** Security Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Expected Time:** 60 mins  
**Experience:** 12+ Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should third-party scripts be governed?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Security is defense in depth: browser controls, secure cookies, CSP, authorization, API security, dependency hygiene and observability.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Configuration Example
```ts
// Architecture-level configuration should be environment driven.
// Never place production secrets in client-side source.

  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```

I would then model failure scenarios, observability and deployment. The final part is trade-offs: what we gain, what complexity we accept, what we defer, and how the architecture can evolve.

## Question 298 — How should security reviews fit into delivery?

**Module:** Security Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Expected Time:** 60 mins  
**Experience:** 12+ Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should security reviews fit into delivery?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Security is defense in depth: browser controls, secure cookies, CSP, authorization, API security, dependency hygiene and observability.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Configuration Example
```ts

// Never place production secrets in client-side source.

  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```

For **How should incident containment work?**, I would first clarify requirements and scale, then separate UI, domain, data and infrastructure boundaries. I would choose state and rendering strategies based on the actual quality attributes, add caching and observability deliberately, secure trusted boundaries, and finish by explaining failure handling and trade-offs.

### 2-Minute Interview Answer
The architecture for **How should incident containment work?** should begin with functional and non-functional requirements. I would define the React/Next.js application boundary, component and feature boundaries, state ownership, API/BFF contracts, caching, authentication, accessibility, performance and observability. I would then walk through a representative request, explain failure recovery and describe how the design scales across traffic and teams. Finally, I would compare alternatives and identify the migration path.

### 5-Minute Deep Explanation
A strong Staff/Principal answer for **How should incident containment work?** is not a technology checklist. It connects business goals to architecture. I would explicitly state assumptions, identify the highest-risk quality attributes, choose boundaries that minimize coupling, define server/client state ownership, design API and cache contracts, and explain security, accessibility and performance as first-class constraints. I would then model failure scenarios, observability and deployment. The final part is trade-offs: what we gain, what complexity we accept, what we defer, and how the architecture can evolve.

## Question 300 — How would you design enterprise frontend security?

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How would you design enterprise frontend security?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements

- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements

- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

- Keyboard navigation

- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

# Module 16 – Accessibility Architecture

## Question 301 — How should an accessibility strategy be defined?

**Module:** Accessibility Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Expected Time:** 60 mins  
**Experience:** 12+ Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should an accessibility strategy be defined?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Accessibility is an architecture concern: semantic primitives, focus rules, keyboard contracts, automated checks and governance should be shared.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Configuration Example
```ts
// Architecture-level configuration should be environment driven.
// Never place production secrets in client-side source.
export const appConfig = {
  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```

### Staff / Principal Discussion
- **Architecture trade-off:** what complexity are we accepting and why?
- **Business decision:** which quality attributes actually affect revenue, retention or compliance?
- **Migration:** how can the existing system move safely?
- **Scaling:** where will the first bottleneck appear?
- **Cost:** what infrastructure or organizational cost does the design create?
- **Developer experience:** how quickly can another team build safely?
- **Governance:** which decisions need platform-level standards?

### Senior Interview Follow-up Questions
1. What would you change at 10× traffic?
2. What breaks first and how would you detect it?
3. What would you cache and how would you invalidate it?
4. What state belongs on the server versus the client?
5. How would you make this accessible?
6. How would you secure the system?
7. How would you migrate a legacy implementation?
8. How would you test the architecture?
9. How would you roll out a risky change?
10. What would you monitor in production?

### Code Review Checklist
- [ ] Clear boundaries
- [ ] No unnecessary global state
- [ ] Typed contracts
- [ ] Security boundaries explicit
- [ ] Accessibility requirements explicit
- [ ] Performance budget considered
- [ ] Failure states modeled
- [ ] Observability included
- [ ] Deployment/rollback strategy defined
- [ ] Migration path documented

### 30-Second Interview Answer
For **How should an accessibility strategy be defined?**, I would first clarify requirements and scale, then separate UI, domain, data and infrastructure boundaries. I would choose state and rendering strategies based on the actual quality attributes, add caching and observability deliberately, secure trusted boundaries, and finish by explaining failure handling and trade-offs.

### 2-Minute Interview Answer
The architecture for **How should an accessibility strategy be defined?** should begin with functional and non-functional requirements. I would define the React/Next.js application boundary, component and feature boundaries, state ownership, API/BFF contracts, caching, authentication, accessibility, performance and observability. I would then walk through a representative request, explain failure recovery and describe how the design scales across traffic and teams. Finally, I would compare alternatives and identify the migration path.

### 5-Minute Deep Explanation
A strong Staff/Principal answer for **How should an accessibility strategy be defined?** is not a technology checklist. It connects business goals to architecture. I would explicitly state assumptions, identify the highest-risk quality attributes, choose boundaries that minimize coupling, define server/client state ownership, design API and cache contracts, and explain security, accessibility and performance as first-class constraints. I would then model failure scenarios, observability and deployment. The final part is trade-offs: what we gain, what complexity we accept, what we defer, and how the architecture can evolve.

### Assignment
Whiteboard **How should an accessibility strategy be defined?** in 45–60 minutes. Produce requirements, HLD, LLD, data flow, API contracts, state decisions, security, performance, observability, deployment, scaling and trade-offs.

### Mock Interview
An interviewer asks: **“Design How should an accessibility strategy be defined? for a global enterprise.”** Spend 5 minutes clarifying requirements, 10 minutes on HLD, 15 minutes on deep dive, 10 minutes on failure/scaling, and 5 minutes on trade-offs.

### Revision Notes
- Requirements before architecture.
- Boundaries before implementation details.
- State ownership must be explicit.
- Cache only with an invalidation strategy.
- Security and accessibility are architecture concerns.
- Performance decisions should be measurable.
- Production architecture includes monitoring and rollback.

## Question 303 — How should keyboard navigation be designed?

**Module:** Accessibility Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Expected Time:** 60 mins  
**Experience:** 12+ Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should keyboard navigation be designed?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Accessibility is an architecture concern: semantic primitives, focus rules, keyboard contracts, automated checks and governance should be shared.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

## Question 305 — How should ARIA be introduced safely?

**Module:** Accessibility Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Expected Time:** 60 mins  
**Experience:** 12+ Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should ARIA be introduced safely?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Accessibility is an architecture concern: semantic primitives, focus rules, keyboard contracts, automated checks and governance should be shared.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

## Question 307 — How should accessible tables be designed?

**Module:** Accessibility Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Expected Time:** 60 mins  
**Experience:** 12+ Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should accessible tables be designed?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Accessibility is an architecture concern: semantic primitives, focus rules, keyboard contracts, automated checks and governance should be shared.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

```text
   ↓
```
```text
Secondary Region
```

### Architecture Decision

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |

| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives

- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches

- excessive bundle growth

- inaccessible interaction states

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

```ts
} as const;
```

### Architecture Decision

| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility

### Performance

Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

- Cache invalidation bugs

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

```ts
  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```

## Question 311 — How should WCAG requirements become engineering standards?

**Module:** Accessibility Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Expected Time:** 60 mins  
**Experience:** 12+ Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should WCAG requirements become engineering standards?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

### Architecture Decision
Accessibility is an architecture concern: semantic primitives, focus rules, keyboard contracts, automated checks and governance should be shared.

### State Management
| State | Preferred Boundary |
|---|---|
| Local UI | React state/reducer |
| Server state | TanStack Query / RTK Query / Apollo |
| Shared client state | Redux Toolkit / Zustand / Jotai when justified |
| URL state | Router/search params |
| Form state | React Hook Form |

### Communication
Use explicit APIs/events between boundaries. For real-time systems define connection lifecycle, ordering, duplication, reconnection and conflict behavior.

### Caching
Define cache ownership, cache key, TTL/staleness policy, invalidation mechanism, privacy boundary and fallback behavior before adding caching.

### Security
Treat browser code as an untrusted execution environment. Authentication identifies the user; authorization must be enforced by trusted backend boundaries.

### Accessibility
Accessibility is part of the architecture rather than a final QA step. Shared primitives should encode keyboard, focus and semantic contracts.

### Performance
Measure before optimizing. Consider SSR/SSG/ISR, streaming, edge delivery, lazy loading, code splitting, tree shaking, caching, virtualization and Core Web Vitals.

### Testing
- Unit tests for deterministic logic
- React Testing Library for behavior
- Playwright for critical user journeys
- Storybook for component states
- Contract/integration tests for API boundaries
- Accessibility automation plus manual review

### Monitoring
Instrument errors, latency, release version, route, device/network context and business-impact signals while respecting privacy requirements.

### Deployment
Use repeatable CI/CD with type checking, linting, tests, build verification, staged promotion, canary/blue-green rollout where justified and rollback automation.

### Scaling
Scale architecture along three axes: runtime traffic, data volume and engineering organization. A design that handles traffic but creates team coupling is not enterprise-scalable.

### Trade-offs
| Decision | Benefit | Cost / Risk |
|---|---|---|
| SSR | Fast content delivery/SEO | Server complexity |
| CSR | Simple client model | Initial UX/SEO trade-offs |
| Micro frontend | Team independence | Runtime/build complexity |
| Monolith | Simpler operations | Larger coordination boundary |
| Global state | Shared access | Coupling/re-render risk |
| Local state | Encapsulation | Duplication if shared incorrectly |
| CDN caching | Lower latency/origin load | Invalidation complexity |

### Alternatives
State the simplest viable alternative, the chosen architecture, and the conditions under which you would switch. Avoid presenting one architecture as universally correct.

### Production Issues
- Cache invalidation bugs
- hydration mismatches
- stale authorization state
- excessive bundle growth
- memory leaks
- retry storms
- inaccessible interaction states
- observability gaps
- release regressions

### Production Considerations
Define ownership, SLIs/SLOs, release strategy, migration plan, incident response, cost boundaries, security review and operational runbooks.

### Reference Implementation
```tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";

type Item = {
  id: string;
  label: string;
};

type Props = {
  items: readonly Item[];
};

export function ExampleFeature({ items }: Props) {
  const [selectedId, setSelectedId] = useState<string | null>(null);

  const selected = useMemo(
    () => items.find((item) => item.id === selectedId) ?? null,
    [items, selectedId],
  );

  return (
    <section aria-label="Example feature">
      <ul>
        {items.map((item) => (
          <li key={item.id}>
            <button
              type="button"
              aria-pressed={selectedId === item.id}
              onClick={() => setSelectedId(item.id)}
            >
              {item.label}
            </button>
          </li>
        ))}
      </ul>

      <p aria-live="polite">
        {selected ? `Selected: ${selected.label}` : "Nothing selected"}
      </p>
    </section>
  );
}
```

### Configuration Example

```ts
  apiBaseUrl: import.meta.env.VITE_API_BASE_URL,
  appVersion: import.meta.env.VITE_APP_VERSION,
} as const;
```

## Question 313 — How should RTL interact with accessibility?

**Module:** Accessibility Architecture  
**Difficulty:** ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ Staff / Principal  
**Expected Time:** 60 mins  
**Experience:** 12+ Years  
**Asked In:** Google • Meta • Amazon • Microsoft • Netflix • Adobe • Airbnb • Stripe • Atlassian • Uber

### Business Problem
Design a production-grade frontend architecture for **How should RTL interact with accessibility?**. The goal is to satisfy business needs while keeping the system scalable, secure, accessible, observable and maintainable.

### Functional Requirements
- Users can access the core capability through a responsive frontend.
- UI state, server state and navigation state have explicit ownership.
- Async operations expose loading, success, empty and failure states.
- The system supports recovery from expected failures.

### Non-functional Requirements
- Maintainable boundaries and clear ownership.
- Responsive performance across realistic devices and networks.
- High availability and graceful degradation.
- Automated testing and production observability.

### Scalability Requirements
- Support growth in users, traffic, data and engineering teams.
- Avoid a single frontend state or package becoming an organizational bottleneck.
- Allow independent feature evolution where useful.

### Performance Requirements
- Optimize initial loading and interaction latency.
- Use CDN/edge caching where appropriate.
- Control JavaScript and rendering cost.
- Virtualize large collections when necessary.

### Security Requirements
- Enforce authorization at trusted server boundaries.
- Minimize sensitive data exposed to client JavaScript.
- Protect sessions, APIs and third-party integrations.
- Apply CSP, secure headers and dependency controls where appropriate.

### Accessibility Requirements
- Semantic HTML
- Keyboard navigation
- Focus management
- Screen-reader support
- Accessible forms, tables and dialogs
- WCAG-oriented automated and manual testing

### SEO Requirements
- Use semantic document structure.
- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.
- Choose SSR/SSG/CSR based on content and product needs.
- Avoid hiding indexable content behind unnecessary client-only rendering.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.

### Failure Scenarios
- API timeout
- Network loss
- Authentication expiry
- Stale cache
- Partial backend failure
- Deployment regression
- Browser/device limitations
- Unexpected client exception

- Define title, metadata and canonical behavior where relevant.

### Offline Requirements
- Define which workflows must work offline.
- Use Service Workers/IndexedDB only where product requirements justify them.
- Queue writes and resolve conflicts explicitly.

### Analytics Requirements
- Track meaningful product events.
- Avoid collecting sensitive data unnecessarily.
- Keep analytics separate from operational telemetry.

### Monitoring Requirements
- Track errors, latency, availability, Core Web Vitals and release health.
- Correlate frontend events with API requests where possible.

### Logging Requirements
- Structured logs.
- Release/version context.
- Request/correlation identifiers when available.
- No secrets or sensitive user content in logs.
